# Suffixes, separators, and excel files
![](/images/file_explorer.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: 5px solid white" fig-align="center"}

You have learnt how to read in .csv and .tsv files.
However, you may encounter text files with other separators or you may even want to read in an excel file.

## File suffixes
![](/images/txt_files.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

There are many types of file suffixes, including:

- .csv: Command Separated Value
- .tsv: Tab Separated Value
- .txt: Text file
- .zip: Compressed file/directory
- .mp3: MPEG-1 Audio Layer III

An important note of file suffixes is that they are arbitrary.
If you change the suffix of a zipped file from .zip to .banana it is still a zip file.
File suffixes are for the benefit of the user and so programs know what type of file the file is.
A music file called "September.banana" will still contain the song data but most media players won't know what to do with it if it does not have the correct file suffix.

## Separators
![](/images/separate.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: 5px solid white" fig-align="center"}

Why is this relevant to you?
Though you may encounter files with the suffix .csv or .tsv and therefore know which separator to use (`,` or `\t`), it is likely you will also encounter .txt files.
Most .txt files will be tab separated (`\t`) but they may also be comma separated (`,`).
Therefore [viewing](/files_subsetting/reading.html) your files can be very useful before reading it in.

Additionally, other file separators that may be used include:

- Space (` `) 
- Tilde (`~`)
- Colon (`:`)
- Semi-colon (`;`)
- Pipe (`|`)


## Excel files
![](/images/readxl.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 5px solid white" fig-align="center"}

You may want to open excel files with R. Normally to do this I open the file in excel and save it as a <u id='csv'>**.csv**</u> or a <u id='tsv'>**.tsv**</u> file and __read__ this into R. Alternatively there are R packages that can directly __read__ in excel files. If this is something you would like to do you can look at the following package:

<https://readxl.tidyverse.org/>

An important note is that __reading__ in a file into R will not change the file. You are creating a new R __object__. Modifying this __object__ will not alter the original file. Later in the materials we will look into how to create new files or overwrite files by __writing__.
